column2: uttering a single sentence brings on great fatigue; he lies awake from breathlessness, cough, illness and exhaustion;
the old man is raised up by one and laid down by another, scorned and slighted by servants, sons and wife;
all his cleanliness gone, he still craves pleasures and food; he is laughed at even by his attendants, and all his kin are weary of him;
remembering the doings of his youth as if they happened in another birth, he sighs long, deeply pained.
Having experienced these and other sorrows in old age, hear too the sorrows he meets in dying.
His neck, feet and hands grow slack and a trembling seizes him; now he is overcome by faintness, now he has a moment of clear awareness.
What will become of my gold, grain, sons, wife, servants and house? — so he is tormented by attachment.
The bonds of his bones are cut by great diseases that pierce the vital points, fierce as saws and as the terrible arrows of Death.
His eyeballs roll, he throws his hands and feet about again and again, his palate, lips and throat dry up, and he rattles in the throat.
His throat is choked, he is tormented by the upward breath, and he is gripped by great burning, thirst and hunger.
Afflicted by Yama's servants, he departs from the body in agony, and then with pain takes on a body made for torment.
These and other terrible sorrows befall men at death; now hear what the dead suffer in hell:
seizure with nooses by Yama's servants, beating with rods, the fearsome sight of Yama and the sight of the dreadful road;
in hells terrible with scalding sand, fire, machines, weapons and the like, torment upon torment, O best of brahmins —
of those being sawn, smelted in crucibles, split with axes and buried in the ground,
impaled on stakes, thrust into tigers' mouths, devoured by vultures and eaten by leopards,
boiled in oil, soaked in caustic mud, hurled down from heights and flung by catapults —
the sorrows that the dwellers of hell suffer in hell, born of sin, O brahmins, are beyond counting.
Not only in hell, O best of brahmins, is there a path of sorrow; even in heaven there is no peace for one who fears to fall and whose merit wanes.
Again a man enters the womb and is born again; again he perishes in the womb, or dies as he is born.
He dies as soon as he is born, or in childhood, or in youth. Whatever thing arises that gives men pleasure, O brahmins,
that very thing becomes the seed of the tree of sorrow. Wife, sons, friends, house, fields, wealth and the rest
do not bring men as much happiness as they bring unhappiness. For those whose minds are scorched by the burning sun of worldly sorrow,
where is there happiness for men except in the shade of the tree of liberation? For this threefold mass of sorrow, the wise hold that
which arises in the states of womb, birth, old age and the rest, the remedy whose sole mark is happiness, a bliss beyond all measure —
attaining the Lord, is held to be the one final remedy; so wise men must strive to attain him.
The means to attain him are said to be knowledge and action, O best of brahmins; and knowledge is said to be of two kinds, arising from scripture and from discrimination.
The Word-Brahman consists of scripture; the Supreme Brahman is born of discrimination. Ignorance is like blind darkness; knowledge from the senses is like a lamp,
and the knowledge born of discrimination, O brahmins, is like the sun. What Manu too said, recalling the meaning of the Veda, O best of sages,
hear it from me in this connection: two Brahmans are to be known — the Word-Brahman and that which is supreme.
One who is versed in the Word-Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman. "Two kinds of knowledge are to be known," says the Atharva scripture:
by the higher the Imperishable is attained; the lower consists of the Rig Veda and the rest. That which is unmanifest, unageing, inconceivable, unborn and imperishable,
indefinable and formless, without hands, feet and the like, all-pervading, eternal, the source of beings, itself without cause,
pervading, by which all is pervaded — that the wise behold. That is Brahman, the supreme abode; that should be meditated on by those who seek liberation.
That subtle one declared by the words of scripture is the supreme abode of Vishnu. He who knows the origin and dissolution of beings, their coming and going,
knowledge and ignorance, is to be called Bhagavan. Knowledge, power, strength, lordship, valour and splendour, without remainder,
are what the word Bhagavan denotes, without any qualities to be rejected. All beings dwell in that Supreme Self,
and he, the Self of all, dwells in beings; therefore he is called Vasudeva. So Prajapati, asked of old by the great sages, told them
the true explanation of the name of the infinite Vasudeva: because he dwells within beings and they dwell in him, and he is the maker and ordainer of the worlds, the Lord is called Vasudeva.
He is the nature of all beings, and though possessing qualities he is beyond all qualities and faults; beyond every covering, the Self of all, by him is filled all the space between the worlds.

His nature is every auspicious quality; with a fraction of his own power he brought forth the creation of beings; taking at will whatever vast body he pleases, he has accomplished the good of the whole world.
A great store of radiance, strength and lordship, the single mass of qualities such as valour and power, higher than the highest, in whom, the Lord of high and low, there are no afflictions at all —
he is the Lord, in individual and collective form, unmanifest in nature and manifest in nature, the Lord of all, the seer of all, the knower of all, possessed of all powers, called the Supreme Lord.
That by which that faultless, pure, supreme, stainless, single-formed one is known, seen or reached is knowledge; all else is called ignorance.
I will tell of the faults that arise as obstacles for one who, out of folly, disregards these places and practises yoga:
deafness, dullness, loss of memory, dumbness, blindness and fever arise at once, born of that ignorance.
Therefore the knower of yoga must always take care in every way, since the body is the means to dharma, wealth, pleasure and liberation.
In a hermitage, a lonely, hidden, silent and fearless place on a mountain, an empty house, a clean and pleasant solitary spot, or a temple,
in the last and first watches of the night, in the forenoon and at midday, well concentrated, moderate in food, with senses conquered,
seated facing east on a pleasant seat, comfortable and steady, neither too low nor too high, free from desire, truthful and pure,
moderate in sleep, anger conquered, devoted to the welfare of all beings, enduring all pairs of opposites, steadfast, with body, feet and head aligned,
placing both hands at the navel, calm, seated in the lotus posture, fixing the gaze on the tip of the nose, restraining the breath and speech,
the sage, drawing the whole group of senses into the heart with the mind, raising the long pranava, mouth closed and perfectly still,
covering the activity of tamas with rajas and of rajas with sattva, and resting in the stainless and calm with eyes closed,
the yogi should constantly unite with the Supreme Person, the giver of liberation, all-pervading and stainless, hidden in the hollow of the heart-lotus.
He should first place the instruments, senses and elements in the knower of the field, and the knower of the field should be joined to the Supreme; so the knower of yoga practises.
For him whose restless mind, abandoning sense objects, comes to rest in the Supreme Self, success in yoga is revealed.
When the mind, free of objects, dissolves into the Supreme Brahman in samadhi, the yogi then attains the supreme state.
When the yogi's mind is unattached to all actions, then, attaining bliss, he reaches nirvana.
Reaching the pure Supreme Person, beyond the three states and called the Fourth, the yogi is liberated by the power of yoga; there is no doubt.
Free from craving for all desires, kindly looking on all, regarding everything as impermanent — so is the yogi liberated, and not otherwise.
The knower of yoga should not indulge the senses; through detachment and constant practice he is liberated, without doubt.
Yoga is not the lotus posture nor gazing at the tip of the nose; yoga is said to be the union of the mind and the senses.
Thus, best of sages, I have told you of yoga, which grants release and is the means of liberation from worldly existence; what else do you wish to hear?
Hearing his words, they said, "Well done, well done," and praising and honouring Vyasa, they prepared to ask him again.
For in all beings, moving and fixed, dwells the one great Self, by whom all this is pervaded.
When the embodied self sees the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, then it attains Brahman.
As far as the Self knowing the Veda extends in oneself, so far does it extend in the Supreme Self; whoever always knows this is fit for immortality.
Even the gods are bewildered on the path of one who has become the Self of all beings and seeks the good of all, seeking the trace of the traceless.
As the track of birds in the sky or of fish in water cannot be seen, so is the path of those who know.
Time cooks all beings in itself by itself; but that in which Time itself is cooked, no one here knows.
It is not above, not across, not below, nor again and again; it is not grasped in the middle; nothing and no one grasps it.
All these worlds are within it; nothing is outside them. Even if one should travel forward like an arrow loosed from the string,
one would never reach the end of the cause, even with the speed of mind. There is nothing subtler than it, and nothing grosser.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and faces everywhere, with ears everywhere in the world, it stands enveloping all.
It is subtler than the subtlest and greater than the greatest; it abides unmoving within all beings yet is not seen.
The imperishable and the perishable — twofold is this nature of the Self: the perishable is in all beings, the divine immortal is the imperishable.
Making the city of nine gates, the Swan (hamsa), controlled and self-mastered, dwells so in all beings, fixed and moving.
The seers of the far shore call the unborn one the Swan because of the abandonment of discriminated bodies and the gathering of new ones.
What is called the Swan is the perishable; what stands unchanging is the imperishable. The knower, attaining the imperishable, gives up life and birth.
O brahmins, since you asked, I have described here truly the Sankhya joined with knowledge.
Now, O brahmins, I will describe the practice of yoga: the unification of intellect and mind and of all the senses,
the knowledge of the all-pervading Self — this is the unsurpassed knowledge. It is to be understood by one who is tranquil, self-controlled, given to inner inquiry,
delighting in the Self, awakened and pure in deeds, having cut away the five faults of yoga known to the wise:
desire, anger, greed, fear and sleep as the fifth. One conquers anger by calm and desire by giving up intentions;
the steadfast one can cut off sleep by cultivating sattva; by firmness he should guard sex and belly, hands and feet by the eye,
eye and ear by the mind, mind and speech by action; he should shed fear through heedfulness, and hypocrisy through serving the wise.
So should he always conquer these faults of yoga, untiring, and always bow to the fires, the brahmins and the gods.
He should avoid arrogant speech, speech joined to violence, and speech that follows passing moods. The seed made of Brahman's radiance, of which all this world is formed —
of that Being of beings the moving and unmoving are seen. Meditation, study, giving, truth, modesty, straightforwardness, forbearance,
cleanliness, purity of self and restraint of the senses — by these radiance grows and sin is driven away.
Equal toward all beings, living on what comes or does not come, with sin shaken off, radiant, eating lightly and with senses conquered,
bringing desire and anger under control, one should resort to the state of Brahman. Collected, making mind and senses one-pointed,
in the early part of the night and the latter, one should fix the mind on the Self. If even one sense of this five-sensed being leaks,
his wisdom flows away like water from the foot of a mountain. First he should seize the mind, as a fisherman catches tortoises,
then the ear, then the eye, tongue and nose; the knower of yoga, restraining these, should set them in the mind,
and likewise, removing intentions, fix the mind in the Self; and so establish the five senses in the mind, and the mind in the heart.
When these, with the mind as sixth, rest in the Self and become serene in that state, then Brahman shines forth.
Like a flame without smoke, radiant like the sun, like lightning's fire in the sky, they behold the Self in the self.
There all is seen everywhere, because it pervades all. Great-souled brahmins who are wise behold it —
steadfast, deeply wise, devoted to the welfare of all beings. Practising thus for a measured time, firm in vows,
sitting alone in solitude, one attains equality with the Imperishable. Confusion, giddiness, whirling, strange smells, sounds and sights,
wondrous tastes and touches, forms of cold, heat and wind, visions and disturbances arising through yoga —
the knower of truth should disregard these and turn them back by equanimity. The sage, restrained, should become familiar with yoga in the three worlds;
he should practise on a mountain peak, at a shrine or at the roots of trees, restraining the group of senses as one keeps goods in a storehouse,
always meditating one-pointedly; through yoga the mind is not disturbed. By whatever means the restless mind can be controlled,
he should apply himself to that and not waver from it. One-pointed, he should seek out empty houses to dwell in.
He should not go beyond bounds in speech, deed or thought; indifferent, restrained in food, he should be the same whether he gains or does not gain.
Toward one who praises him and one who salutes him he should be equal, and should not dwell on good or ill.
He should not rejoice at gains nor brood over losses; equal toward all beings, he should be like the wind.
For such a good man, whose self is at ease, who sees equally everywhere and is ever yoked, the Word-Brahman is surpassed within six months.
Seeing others afflicted by pain, regarding a clod, a stone and gold as the same, one devoted to this path should not turn from it in confusion.
Even one of low birth, or a woman who seeks dharma — they too may reach the highest goal by this path.

Beholding him who is unborn, ancient, unageing and eternal, beyond the senses and beyond their reach, O brahmins, the wise attain this equality with the Supreme Being, the goal from which there is no return.
Making the mind, perfected by knowledge, supreme in meditation, free from lordship and peaceful, one then goes to the supreme abode.
But a mortal who is subject to all the senses, whose memory wavers, meets death by giving himself up to them.
Striking down all intentions, one should fix the mind in sattva; having fixed the mind in sattva, one then overcomes time.
Through clarity of mind the ascetic here gives up good and bad; serene, abiding in the Self, he enjoys endless happiness.
The mark of that clarity is like the happiness of deep sleep, or like a lamp that burns without flickering in a windless place.
So, yoking himself by himself in the early and late parts of the night, eating lightly and pure of self, he sees the Self in the self.
This teaching for sons, the secret of all the Vedas, not based on tradition or scripture but self-verifying, is this scripture.
Whatever treasure there is in all the tales of dharma and of truth, churned for ten thousand years, this nectar has been drawn out —
as butter from curd and fire from wood, so the knowledge of the wise has been drawn out for the sake of liberation.
This scripture, a teaching for sons, is to be told to graduates of Vedic study; it should not be told to one who is not tranquil, not self-controlled, nor to an ascetic without these,
nor to one ignorant of the Veda, nor to one who does not follow, nor to the envious or the crooked, nor to one who does not do as instructed,
nor to one burnt by the science of disputation, nor to a slanderer. To one who is praiseworthy and deserves praise, to the tranquil ascetic,
to a dear son or a devoted disciple should this secret dharma be told, and to no one else in any way.
Even if a man should give him this whole earth full of jewels, the knower of truth should consider this teaching better.
Therefore that more secret matter, the superhuman teaching on the Self, seen by the great sages and sung in the Vedanta —
that I give to you, since you ask me, good ones. What was in my mind and whatever doubt was in your hearts, you have heard it all; what else shall I tell you?"
Tell us again, in detail, about the Self, so that we may understand it as it is, blessed one, best of sages.

The teaching on the Self of man that is recited here, O brahmins, I will tell you; take in its explanation.
brahmapuran:237:45	Earth, water, fire, wind and space are the great elements, and the maker of beings is in all beings.
brahmapuran:237:46	How should one describe space and the rest within bodies, when one who has a form does not see the body in it? And how should one discern the qualities of the senses?
brahmapuran:237:47	This I will describe to you as it truly appears; listen here with attention, as it is and as it truly stands.
brahmapuran:237:48	Sound, the ear and the cavities — these three are the marks of space; breath, movement and touch — these three are qualities of wind;
brahmapuran:237:49	form, the eye and digestion — fire is set down as threefold; taste, the tongue and sweat — these three are qualities of water;
brahmapuran:237:50	what is smelled, the nose and the body — these three are qualities of earth. Such is the group of senses, explained as made of the five elements.
brahmapuran:237:51	Touch is said to belong to wind, taste to water and form to fire; sound arises from space, and smell is known as the quality of earth.
brahmapuran:237:52	Mind, intellect and one's own nature — these qualities arise from their own source; they pass beyond the qualities and are held to be higher than them.
brahmapuran:237:53	As a tortoise extends its limbs and draws them in, so the best of intellects restrains the group of senses.
brahmapuran:237:54	What one sees above the soles of the feet and below and above the head — in this very function the excellent intellect operates.
brahmapuran:237:55	The intellect is led by the qualities, and the intellect leads the senses too, all six with the mind; without the intellect, where would the qualities be?
brahmapuran:237:56	Men have five senses; the sixth is called the mind; the intellect they call the seventh, and know the knower of the field as the eighth.
brahmapuran:237:57	The eye is only for seeing; the mind creates doubt; the intellect is for determination; the knower of the field is called the witness.
brahmapuran:237:58	Rajas, tamas and sattva — these three arise from their own source and are alike in all beings; one should recognize these qualities.
brahmapuran:237:59	Whatever one notices in oneself joined with joy, as if calm and serene, one should recognize as sattva.
brahmapuran:237:60	Whatever is joined with agitation in body or mind should likewise be recognized as rajas at work.
brahmapuran:237:61	Whatever is joined with delusion, obscure and uneven, beyond reasoning and unknowable, one should recognize as tamas.
brahmapuran:237:62	Delight, joy, bliss, mastery and a calm, healthy mind, whether they arise without cause or from a cause, are called the qualities of sattva.
brahmapuran:237:63	Pride, false speech, greed, delusion and impatience — these are the signs of rajas, operating through their causes.
brahmapuran:237:64	Delusion, heedlessness, lethargy, and sleep from which one does not wake, whenever they occur, are to be known as the qualities of tamas.
brahmapuran:237:65	The mind puts forth ideas, the intellect determines, and the heart wills what is dear: threefold is the impulse to action.
brahmapuran:237:66	Beyond the senses are their objects, beyond the objects is the mind, beyond the mind is the intellect, and beyond the intellect is known the Self.
brahmapuran:237:67	The intellect is man's self; the intellect alone leads the self. When it produces an idea, it becomes mind.
brahmapuran:237:68	Because the senses are distinct, the intellect transforms itself accordingly: hearing, it becomes the ear; touching, it is called touch;
brahmapuran:237:69	seeing, it becomes sight; tasting, it becomes the tongue; smelling, it becomes the nose — so the intellect transforms itself distinctly.
brahmapuran:237:70	These they call the senses; through their activity it abides. The intellect abides in the Person, established in the state of intellect.
brahmapuran:237:71	Sometimes it finds joy, sometimes it grieves, and sometimes here it is neither happy nor sad but bewildered.
brahmapuran:237:72	Itself made of states, it passes beyond these three states, as the ocean, lord of rivers, with its waves passes beyond its great shore.
brahmapuran:237:73	When it longs for something, it becomes mind. With the intellect one should consider these separately in their seats,
brahmapuran:237:74	and the senses, which are pure, should be examined completely, all of them in order, as each is prescribed.
brahmapuran:237:75	The intellect with undivided mind is a state that abides in the mind; when it is active it is rajas, and it also goes beyond sattva.
brahmapuran:237:76	Those who operate through these states, in all these three, move along after objects like spokes around the rim of a chariot wheel.
brahmapuran:237:77	One should make the mind a lamp, with the senses led by the intellect going forth as fits, indifferent and at ease.
brahmapuran:237:78	Knowing 'Such is the nature of this,' one is not deluded; neither grieving nor exulting, always free from envy.
brahmapuran:237:79	The Self cannot be seen by the senses that range among desires, many, active, hard to hold, belonging to the undisciplined.
brahmapuran:237:80	But when one rightly restrains their reins with the mind, then the Self shines forth, as a shape lit by a lamp.
brahmapuran:237:81	As, when darkness departs, everything becomes visible to all beings, so should this be understood.
brahmapuran:237:82	As a water bird moving in the water is not wetted by it, so the yogi whose self is freed is not stained by the faults of the qualities.
brahmapuran:237:83	So too one of perfected wisdom, moving among sense objects without faults and unattached to all, is in no way stained.
brahmapuran:237:84	He who has abandoned the karma done before and ever delights in the Self, who has become the Self of all beings, though associated with the qualities,
brahmapuran:237:85	the Self itself never gives birth to the qualities. The qualities do not know the Self; the Self always knows the qualities.
brahmapuran:237:86	He is the overseer and true seer of the qualities. Thus a man should discern the difference between sattva and the knower of the field.
brahmapuran:237:87	One creates the qualities, the other does not create them; by nature these two are separate, yet always joined —
brahmapuran:237:88	as gold is joined with stone, or as the gnat and the fig are joined together,
brahmapuran:237:89	or as the reed within the munja grass is both separate and together — so these two are united, each established in the other.
brahmapuran:238:17	Restraining with the intellect, in truth, the tormenting senses that have spread out in every direction, as a father restrains his young children —
brahmapuran:238:18	one-pointedness of mind and senses is the highest austerity; it is to be known as higher than all dharmas and is called the supreme dharma.
brahmapuran:238:19	Gathering all of them, with the mind as sixth, through wisdom, he remained content in the Self, not thinking of the many things to be thought of.
brahmapuran:238:20	When the senses, turned back from their objects, remain in their abode, then by yourself you will see the supreme, eternal Self.
brahmapuran:238:21	The wise brahmins behold the great Self, the Self of all, like a fire without smoke.
brahmapuran:238:22	As a great tree with many branches, laden with flowers and fruits, does not itself know where its flowers are or where its fruits,
brahmapuran:238:23	so the individual self does not know where it will go or where it came from; there is another, its inner Self, who sees all.
brahmapuran:238:24	With the blazing lamp of knowledge one sees the Self by the self. Having seen the Self, O brahmins, become free of passion,
brahmapuran:238:25	released from all sins like snakes that have cast their skins; attaining supreme understanding here, be free of anxiety and fever.
brahmapuran:238:26	The terrible river that flows through the world, with currents on every side, with the five senses as its crocodiles and the mind's intentions as its banks,
brahmapuran:238:27	covered with the grass of greed and delusion, with desire and anger as its serpents, truth as its landing place and falsehood as its turbulence, anger as its mud — that best of rivers,
brahmapuran:238:28	rising from the unmanifest, swift, full of desire and anger — cross that river by the intellect, hard for the undisciplined to cross,
brahmapuran:238:29	flowing to the ocean of worldly existence, with the netherworld of births hard to pass, arising from one's own birth, hard to approach with the whirlpool of the tongue.
brahmapuran:238:30	The wise, of perfected understanding and steadfast, cross it; having crossed it, one is free on every side, cleansed, self-possessed and pure,
brahmapuran:238:31	and resting in the highest understanding becomes fit for union with Brahman; having crossed beyond all afflictions, serene and stainless,
brahmapuran:238:32	looking on beings of every place as if from a height, neither angry nor elated, and without cruelty of mind,
brahmapuran:238:33	then you will see the origin and dissolution of all beings. This the wise have held to be superior to all dharmas —
brahmapuran:238:34	this dharma, O best of those who uphold dharma, sages who see the truth, of the all-pervading Self, O brahmins; such is the teaching for sons.
brahmapuran:238:35	It should be told to one who is restrained, well-meaning and devoted. This knowledge of the Self is secret, the greatest and most secret of all.
brahmapuran:238:36	What I have told you, O brahmins, is plainly witnessed by the Self itself. Brahman is neither woman nor man, nor is it neuter;
brahmapuran:238:37	Brahman is without sorrow and without pleasure, the essence of past, future and present. Knowing it, neither man nor woman comes to birth again.
brahmapuran:238:38	As all the doctrines are, so have I told these as they are, O brahmins; they are and they are not.
brahmapuran:238:39	This is what a father, glad at heart, would tell his son, seeing his good — a son full of love, endowed with virtues, and with the kindness of a good son.
brahmapuran:238:40	The Grandsire declared that liberation comes through a means, not without one; we wish to hear that means duly, O sage."

That is fitting in you, O wise ones — a subtle insight, that you always seek all aims through a means, sinless ones.
brahmapuran:238:42	The intention to make a pot's tools is not held to be the making of the pot; so the means to dharma and the rest is not the cause in other dharmas.
brahmapuran:238:43	The path to the eastern sea does not lead to the western; there is one path to liberation — hear it from me, sinless ones.
brahmapuran:238:44	By forbearance one should cut off anger, and desire by giving up intentions; the steadfast should cut off sleep by cultivating sattva.
brahmapuran:238:45	By heedfulness one should guard against fear, and guard the field and awareness; by firmness one should turn back longing, aversion and desire.
brahmapuran:238:46	The knower of truth should overcome sleep and wandering fancy by the practice of knowledge, and the yogi should overcome disturbances by wholesome, digestible and measured food;
brahmapuran:238:47	greed and delusion by contentment, sense objects by seeing the truth; he should conquer adharma by compassion, and dharma by indifference;
brahmapuran:238:48	hope by thought for the future, power by giving up attachment, affection by seeing impermanence, and hunger by yoga — so the wise one should;
brahmapuran:238:49	the self by compassion, craving by contentment; he should conquer lethargy by exertion and doubt by resolution;
brahmapuran:238:50	much talk by silence, and fear by courage. He should restrain speech and mind by the intellect, and that by the eye of knowledge;
brahmapuran:238:51	the great self should restrain knowledge, and the peace of the Self should restrain that. This is to be understood by one who is calm and pure in deeds,
brahmapuran:238:52	having cut away the five faults of yoga known to the wise — desire, anger, greed, fear and sleep as the fifth.
brahmapuran:238:53	Having abandoned these, one should practise the means of yoga duly: meditation, study, giving, truth, modesty, straightforwardness, forbearance,
brahmapuran:238:54	cleanliness in conduct, purity and restraint of the senses — by these radiance grows and sin is struck down.
brahmapuran:238:55	His intentions are fulfilled and understanding arises; with sin shaken off, radiant, eating lightly and with senses conquered,
brahmapuran:238:56	bringing desire and anger under control, he should enter the state of Brahman. Freedom from delusion, freedom from attachment, the giving up of desire and anger,
brahmapuran:238:57	freedom from dejection and from excitement, freedom from agitation, and steadiness — this is the path of liberation, serene, stainless and pure; and so too are the disciplines of speech, body and mind, undecaying when kept willingly.
As a small, weak fire is put out, O brahmins, when smothered by heavy fuel, so is the power of yoga said to be when weak.
That same fire, O brahmins, when it gains strength again and is fanned by the wind, may quickly burn this whole earth.
The yogi strong in knowledge of truth, blazing with radiance and of great strength, could dry up the whole world like the sun at the end of time.
As a weak man is carried away by a current, O brahmins, so a yogi without strength is carried away by sense objects.
But as an elephant stems that same current, so, having gained the strength of yoga, one is not carried away by sense objects.
Endowed with the power of yoga, through their mastery the lords of yoga enter at will all the Prajapatis, the Manus and the great elements.
Neither Yama, nor wrathful Death the Ender, nor Mrityu of terrible prowess can overcome the yogi of boundless radiance, O brahmins.
Having gained power, O best of brahmins, the yogi may create many thousands of selves and roam the earth with all of them;
with some he may enjoy sense objects, and with others perform fierce austerity, and then withdraw them again, O brahmins, as the sun withdraws its rays.
For one established in the power of yoga, O best of sages, Vishnu, the source of liberation, is surely attained.
These powers taught in yoga I have told you, O best of brahmins, as examples; now I will speak again of subtle ones, O brahmins.
Hear, O best of sages, the subtle illustrations concerning the concentration of the self and the practice of fixation.
As an archer, heedful and collected, hits his target, so the yogi rightly yoked attains liberation, without doubt.
As a man carrying a full vessel of oil, his mind fixed and unwavering, climbs a stair with attentive mind,
so the liberated one makes the self and his yoga perfectly steady, and makes the self stainless, like the sun to behold.
As a steersman, attentive, O best of brahmins, quickly brings a ship on the great ocean to port with its passengers,
so the knower of yoga, joined in yoga through concentration of the self, reaches a place hard to attain on leaving this body, O brahmins.
As a charioteer, attentive and well collected, quickly brings a bowman, a bull among men, with good horses to the desired place,
so, O brahmins, the yogi collected in fixations quickly reaches the supreme place, like an arrow loosed at its mark.
He who, entering the Self with the self, remains unmoving, reaches the unageing state, as a fish breaks free of the net.
At the navel, the head, the belly, the heart, the chest, the sides, in sight, hearing or smell, he of boundless power —
the yogi who, collected in great vows, rightly joins the subtle Self with the self in these places, O best of brahmins,
very quickly burns up karma, good and bad, massive as a mountain, and resting in the highest yoga is released whenever he wishes."
By taking what kinds of food and conquering what, O good one, does the yogi gain power? Please tell us that.

Given to eating broken grains and oil-cake, O brahmins, and avoiding oily foods, the yogi gains power.
